conclusion: Full heuristic-only warmup with block reward 0.15 produced the strongest robust model; lower/higher nearby coefficients and mixture schedules did not surpass it. The 0.25 attempt and all three conservative attempt-4 mixtures are status-1 incomplete and cannot be ranked as terminal results; attempt-2 and mixture waves also changed mistake or mixture schedules. The 0.1/0.25/0.4 sweep is controlled but the 0.15 result uses a later, longer warmup configuration. Champion means best among the 61 recorded MLflow runs under the stated heuristic-evaluation criterion, not proven superiority against learned agents or across seeds. It is a single completed run, and its run name date differs from the actual MLflow September 2026 start.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Attempt 1: test whether a 0.15 block reward raises full-duration heuristic-only warmup performance.

results_insights.insight: The completed 0.15 run reached 47% average win rate.
Its 18% floor showed much broader robustness than many earlier curricula.
The limiting combined-O matchup won 18% over 9.51-move games.
The weakest combined-O matchup was not merely represented by missing or truncated evaluation.

reasoning: A 0.15 block coefficient was the strongest completed attempt-1 setting on average and worst rate.
The full heuristic-only horizon likely reinforced broad evaluator-specific competence.
Single-run comparisons cannot separate seed variance, and later attempts alter other curriculum knobs.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Attempt 1: test whether increasing block reward from 0.15 to 0.20 improves full-duration warmup.

results_insights.insight: The 0.20 variant trailed 0.15 by 10.5 percentage points.
Its robustness floor trailed 0.15 by 11 points.
Combined-O was limiting, over 11.16-move games.
Longer limiting games did not yield more wins than block15.

reasoning: Increasing block reward to 0.20 overemphasized blocking relative to winning competence.
The controlled one-knob comparison favors 0.15 on average and worst metrics.
Unreplicated PPO variation remains a plausible secondary explanation.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Attempt 1: test 0.25 block reward, qualified because the run was interrupted before the 15.36M-step target.

results_insights.insight: At interruption, average win rate was 2.33%; this is not a terminal 15.36M comparison.
The partial checkpoint had a zero-win matchup.
Defensive-X was 8% over 18.46-move games at the partial checkpoint.
Episode-length evidence is also partial.

reasoning: The run was interrupted at roughly one fifth of its target horizon, so low values cannot rank the final 0.25 setting.
High block reward may slow early learning, but completion is required to test that explanation.
Checkpoint noise and unequal horizon dominate any comparison with completed block15/block20 runs.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Attempt 1: test whether 0.4 defensive-opening probability improves the block20 warmup control.

results_insights.insight: More openings improved average by 2.17 percentage points over block20.
The floor improved from 7% to 9%.
Combined-O remained limiting, over 11.58-move games.
The weakest matchup remained moderate length.

reasoning: More defensive openings modestly improved both average and floor at block20.
The controlled one-knob delta supports a curriculum-opening benefit.
The gain is small enough that replication would be needed before treating it as reliable.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Attempt 1: test whether very slight potential shaping improves the block20 warmup control.

results_insights.insight: Shaping reduced average by 6.33 percentage points.
The floor fell from 7% to 3%.
Combined-O was limiting, over 10.89-move games.
The weak combined-O evidence is paired with complete episode lengths.

reasoning: Even 0.0025 potential shaping harmed this block-reward warmup regimen.
The controlled comparison aligns with earlier shaping dead ends.
Single-run variance remains, but average and worst metrics both moved adversely.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Attempt 2: test whether ending at a higher 0.3 opponent mistake rate improves the strong block15 setting.

results_insights.insight: The higher final mistake rate trailed attempt-1 block15's 47% average.
Its floor was only 5% versus 18% for block15.
Offensive-O was strong, with 6.86-move games, but other matchups limited robustness.
The offensive-O evidence was based on short complete games.

reasoning: Keeping opponents more mistake-prone late did not preserve broad robustness.
The two-parameter attempt framing versus block15 means both ticket wave and opponent trajectory matter.
Single-seed variation could contribute, but the 13-point worst-rate drop is substantial.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Attempt 2: test whether reducing block reward below 0.15 improves full-duration warmup.

results_insights.insight: Block10 reached 41.33%, below block15 but above other attempt-2 variants.
Its 12% floor was second only to block15 among completed ticket runs.
Combined-O was limiting over 7.89-move games.
The weakest games were relatively short.

reasoning: A moderate 0.10 block reward retained broad competence better than higher 0.20 and lower 0.05 settings.
Block15 still led, suggesting an optimum around 0.10-0.15.
Attempt waves and unreplicated seeds limit precise coefficient ranking.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Attempt 2: test whether a minimal 0.05 block reward is sufficient for strong full-duration warmup.

results_insights.insight: Block05 substantially underperformed block10 and block15.
Its floor was only 5%.
Combined-O remained weak over 6.07-move games.
Weak combined-O games ended quickly.

reasoning: A 0.05 coefficient supplied too little defensive learning signal for broad competence.
The completed coefficient sweep favors an intermediate 0.10-0.15 range.
Unreplicated seeds mean the exact magnitude is uncertain, but both average and floor were worse.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Attempt 3: test whether a balanced three-heuristic mix fading toward combined improves block10 warmup.

results_insights.insight: The balanced mix trailed the single-combined block10 run by 13.33 points.
Its floor collapsed from 12% to 1%.
Offensive-X was strong, but combined-X was only 1%.
The strong offensive-X result occurred over short 6.5-move games.
Combined-X failures occurred over moderate-length games.

reasoning: The balanced mixture created specialist offensive competence at the cost of combined robustness.
Curriculum interference between heuristic objectives likely reduced transferable play.
This changes the opponent representation and schedule together relative to attempt 2, so only within-attempt mix comparisons are clean.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Attempt 3: test whether defense-biased initial three-heuristic exposure improves the balanced-to-combined schedule.

results_insights.insight: Defense bias reduced average versus the balanced mix.
The floor improved from 1% to 5% despite lower average.
Defensive-X remained weak over 20.76-move games.
Longer defensive-X games did not yield high win rate.

reasoning: Initial defense bias traded aggregate performance for a modestly better worst-case floor.
Exposure to defensive games did not directly translate to high defensive evaluator win rates.
The one-schedule-vector comparison is controlled, but stochastic seed effects remain.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Attempt 3: test whether offense-biased initial three-heuristic exposure improves the balanced-to-combined schedule.

results_insights.insight: Offense bias was the strongest attempt-3 mix at 35% average.

Strong offensive-X wins occurred quickly.

reasoning: Offense-biased exposure best supported average competence among attempt-3 mixtures.
The schedule over-specialized on offensive matchups and failed to raise the worst-case floor.
The controlled vector comparison is informative, though it remains a single seed.
